front: What is the usual copper Ethernet channel limit, and what must you check?
back: 100 m for the specified category on supporting ports, commonly 90 m installed plus 10 m patch leads. Some copper modules have shorter limits.

front: Cable choices for 1 Gbps and for a full 100 m 10GBASE-T channel?
back: Cat5e or better is the normal new 1 Gbps choice. Use Cat6A for 10GBASE-T at 100 m on supporting interfaces.

front: Which pin groups form the four physical twisted pairs?
back: 1–2, 3–6, 4–5 and 7–8. A split pair can pass simple pin continuity while using the wrong physical pairing.

front: Which pairs does a conventional 10/100 crossover exchange?
back: Pins 1–2 exchange with pins 3–6: 1↔3 and 2↔6. This is the 10/100 crossover mapping, not a complete rule for every four-pair interface.

front: Without auto-MDIX, when is crossover used on traditional 10/100 ports?
back: Between like electrical arrangements: switch–switch or PC–router, for example. PC/router/server–switch uses straight-through.

front: How does a rollover console cable differ from an Ethernet cable?
back: A traditional rollover reverses pins for a serial console connection. Connect it to the Console port; similar-looking connectors do not make it Ethernet.

front: How do single-mode and multimode fiber differ?
back: Single-mode has a smaller core and commonly supports longer-distance optical designs. Multimode has a larger core and commonly serves shorter links; use specifications, not jacket color alone.

front: What do common 1 Gbps SFP and 10 Gbps SFP+ examples teach about module choice?
back: Match form factor, supported port speed, Ethernet optical standard and fiber. Physical fit and matching connectors alone do not establish compatibility.

front: Hub versus switch: collision and broadcast domains?
back: A hub's devices share one collision domain. A switch separates port segments, while ports in one VLAN share a broadcast domain. Full-duplex Ethernet has no normal collisions.

front: What can an automatic 10/100 end do when its peer is forced to 100/full?
back: Detect 100 Mbps but not the forced duplex setting, then operate at half duplex. The resulting link can be up with a duplex mismatch.

front: What evidence supports a duplex-mismatch diagnosis?
back: Opposing operational duplex settings at the two ends. Collisions/late collisions or received-frame errors may support it, but counters alone are not conclusive.

front: What does the a- prefix in a-full or a-100 mean?
back: The setting was selected automatically, rather than explicitly forced. It can reflect negotiation or sensed/defaulted behavior, so compare both ends.

front: Administrative shutdown versus a lost physical link: what evidence matters?
back: Administratively down identifies the local shutdown. A down/notconnect state can have several causes, including the far end; inspect both ends.
Runts are undersized Ethernet frames. Giants exceed the permitted frame size for that interface and encapsulation; tags and larger configured frames affect the limit.

front: What does a late collision suggest on a half-duplex 10/100 link?
back: A collision occurred beyond the permitted window. Investigate duplex agreement and physical/hardware conditions; it is not proof of one specific defect.

front: What do increasing output drops commonly suggest?
back: An egress queue cannot hold all offered traffic. Examine load and queue behavior; drops do not automatically prove a cable fault.

front: Is −16 dBm within a supplied receive range of −12 through −1 dBm?
back: No. −16 dBm is lower power than the −12 dBm limit. Check transmitter, path, connectors, distance and compatibility; the reading alone does not isolate the cause.

front: How do you restore automatic speed and duplex in interface configuration?
back: Use speed auto and duplex auto on both supported ends. Verify matching operational settings and a fresh traffic test.
